# Terrain

The shape of the land as a height map, where it comes from, and how real elevation data becomes game land.

Headers: `poligon/world/height_map.h`, `poligon/world/terrain.h`, `poligon/world/terrain_generator.h`. Tool: `terrain_tool`. Examples: `examples/world/terrain`, `examples/world/terrain_generator`. Tests: `tests/world/height_map_test.cpp`, `tests/world/terrain_render_test.cpp`, `tests/world/terrain_generator_test.cpp`.

**State:** land is generated by simulating uplift, river and slope erosion, raindrops and lakes, together with maps of water, flow, moisture, sediment and rock; it is drawn to the horizon with levels of detail, with up to eight ground layers chosen by those maps, lit and shadowed like everything else, and physics collides with it. Lakes are water surfaces (`poligon/world/water.h`). Not yet: streams as water, smoothing of the change between patch sizes, plants placed by rules.

## Drawing

```cpp
poligon::TerrainConfig config;
config.origin = {-3000.0f, -280.0f, -3000.0f};       // world position of the map's first point
config.material.colors = renderer.CreateTextureArray(layer_colors, 4);         // one image per layer
config.material.normals = renderer.CreateTextureArray(layer_normals, 4, data); // data: is_color = false
config.material.layer_count = 4;
config.material.weights[0] = renderer.CreateTexture(weights[0], data);         // from MakeTerrainLayerWeights
poligon::Terrain terrain(renderer, height_map, config);
// every frame, between BeginFrame and EndFrame:
terrain.Draw(camera);
```

- The land is not one mesh. It is drawn as square **patches** from a tree of squares: the whole map is one square; a square nearer to the camera than its size times `TerrainConfig::detail` is split into four, down to the smallest size (64 cells of the height map). Under the camera there is a vertex per map point; a hillside kilometers away is a few coarse squares. A 6 x 6 km map with a point every meter is 36 million points and is drawn with a few hundred patches.
- Every patch is the same flat grid mesh of 64 x 64 cells. The vertex shader (`terrain.vert.hlsl`) lifts each vertex to the land's height, read from an image that holds the whole map on the graphics card (16 bits per point: 72 MB for 6000 x 6000). No mesh is ever built from the map.
- Where a fine patch meets a coarse one, their edges do not match exactly. Each patch has a **skirt**, a rim hanging down, that hides the gaps.
- The direction the ground faces is worked out per pixel from the height image (`terrain.frag.hlsl`), so distant coarse patches are shaded as finely as near ones.
- Look (`TerrainMaterial`): up to eight ground layers mixed by weight images (see Ground layers below); each texture is read at its own size and seven times larger, and the larger reading takes over with distance, which hides the repetition; slopes between `steep_start_degrees` and `steep_end_degrees` fade to `steep_color`.
- Lighting is shared with meshes (`lighting.hlsli`): sun, shadows in all four cascades, sky light, ambient occlusion, fog.
- `Terrain::GetHeight(x, z)`, `GetNormal`, `GetSlopeDegrees` answer for world positions; `GetStats()` counts patches by size.
- Under `Terrain` is `Renderer::CreateTerrain` / `DrawTerrain(terrain, material, patches, count)`; all patches of a call cost one draw call per pass and each is culled on its own.

## What hills hide

`TerrainOcclusion` (`poligon/world/terrain_occlusion.h`) leaves out of the picture what the land hides (occlusion culling by terrain). Our own code: no library covers a height field seen from one point and tested against boxes on the processor.

- The horizon: from the camera, in 512 directions, the land is followed out to 4096 m in steps of half the floor's spacing (32 m), and each step keeps the steepest slope (rise over distance) of the land so far. Built on the processor, rebuilt only when the camera has moved more than 0.25 m; deterministic, nothing is read back from the graphics card.
- It is built from `LandInfo::occlusion_floor`: at the background's points (64 m apart), the lowest height of the land within 64 m of each (over the four squares around it; `MakeOcclusionFloor`, made when the land is cooked, `poligon-world 2`). Blended between its points it never rises above the land, so the horizon may be lower than the real one, never higher, and nothing visible is left out. Ridges narrower than about 128 m are lost from it.
- `IsHidden(box)`: true when the box lies below the horizon in every direction its footprint covers, measured only against land nearer than the box (two steps of margin); its steepest slope from the eye is that of its top at its nearest distance (top above the eye) or its farthest (top below).
- `Vegetation::SetOcclusion` and `Terrain::SetOcclusion`: hidden plant cells and land squares are drawn as shadow casters only, as cells out of view already were (`InstanceOptions::draw_in_view` false; `Renderer::DrawTerrain` takes the options too), so shadows do not change. Counted in `VegetationStats::cells_hidden_by_terrain` and `TerrainStats::patches_hidden`. `forest_scene` uses it for the trees, the ground cover and the land; the word `noocclusion` turns it off, and it prints what was hidden.
- Gain on the GTX 980 at 1920 x 1080 (800 frames, with against without): 0 to 0.1 ms in medium and 0.1 to 0.3 ms in high in the four measured views and two views with a ridge in front (`0 400 0 0`: 1511 of 4140 cells hidden; `400 -400 180 0`: 926). Small, because what hills hide here is mostly far trees drawn as impostors, already cheap; it will matter more with more detail far away.
- Test: `tests/world/terrain_occlusion_test.cpp` (the floor never rises above the land; behind a hill 50 m high and 300 m wide a box is hidden, in front of it not, a tower rising above its top not, nothing without a floor; a plant cell behind it is not drawn in the picture while the one in front is: 4 instances in view of 8; both backends).

## Physics

- `PhysicsWorld::AddHeightField(heights, size, spacing, origin)` makes ground from a square grid of heights. A walking character, bodies and rays treat it like any other ground.
- For a large map, give physics only the part where things happen (`CropHeightMap`): `forest_scene` uses 1 x 1 km around the player's start, with fences at its edge.

## In forest_scene

`forest_scene` generates the default land on its first run and loads it from `build/terrain_cache` afterwards. The player starts on gentle ground 150 to 500 m from the largest lake, as high above it as possible (up to 40 m) while the lake's middle stays in view, looking at it; the world's origin is there. Seven ground layers follow the maps: mossy forest floor everywhere, dry litter in patches on drier ground, grass in clearings, mud where water gathers and along the shore, sand and gravel on the shore line and in shallow water, small stones on the lake bed, rock on steep ground. Undergrowth and rocks stand within 250 m of the start and big trees continue to 1200 m, none on slopes over 33 degrees or in a lake, with a clearing from the start down to the lake. The lakes are water surfaces (`CreateLakeSurfaces`, see the water stage in [rendering.md](rendering.md)). Trees cast shadows up to 65 m. (Choosing the start, the clearing and the layer rules are the scene's own choices; plant rules that read the maps are the next steps.)

## Generated land

Header: `poligon/world/terrain_generator.h`. Example: `examples/world/terrain_generator`. Test: `tests/world/terrain_generator_test.cpp`. Since 2026-10-15 `forest_scene` stands on generated land; the Batorz data and the TIFF reader stay.

The generator simulates the processes that shape real land instead of adding noise. No library fitted (checked on 2026-10-15: fastscapelib is GPL-3, RichDEM has no license, SimpleHydrology is MIT but makes no lakes, FastNoise2 is MIT but its SIMD paths are not bit-repeatable), so it is our own code after these publications:

1. **Large scale**, on a coarse grid (`coarse_spacing`, 4 m): the run starts from older rolling hills (`initial_relief`, `initial_hill_size`). The crust rises (`uplift`, 55 to 100% of it in broad patches); rivers cut in by the stream power law E = K A^m S (`erodibility`, `area_exponent`), solved implicitly from the outlets upstream (Braun and Willett 2013), so any time step is stable; slopes creep (`hillslope_diffusion`); water routes over the land with every hollow filled to its rim (Priority-Flood with epsilon, Barnes, Lehman and Mulla 2014), and sediment carried into a filled hollow settles there. Late in the run (`basin_start`) a few irregular basins stop rising (`basin_count`, `basin_radius`, `basin_sinking`), as land does over faults or melting ice; lakes form in them. Outlet edges (`outlet_edges`) stand for land that goes on beyond the map: they keep the old hills' heights and rise slowly, so no cliff forms along them. The result is scaled to `relief` meters.
2. **Fine scale**, on the height grid (`spacing`, 1 m): the coarse land is interpolated (Catmull-Rom), gets bumps of `detail_height` (smaller on flat ground), loose material slides wherever the slope passes `talus_degrees` (thermal erosion, Musgrave, Kolb and Mace 1989), then `droplets_per_square_meter` raindrops run downhill for up to `droplet_steps` meters, cutting rills and gullies and dropping material where they slow down (Beyer 2015). Each drop's speed and its cut per step are limited, and erosion fades out near the map's edge: without that a steep wall feeds itself into a pit hundreds of meters deep (it happened once, on the full map).
3. **Maps**, on the map grid (`map_spacing`, 2 m): `water_level` (the lakes: hollows filled to their rims, kept if at least `min_lake_area` and `min_lake_depth`; the level reaches one point past the shore so that the shore follows the 1 m heights), `flow` (square meters that drain through each point, routed through lakes), `moisture` (from the topographic wetness index ln(a / tan slope), Beven and Kirkby 1979, raised near water), `sediment` (meters laid down by lakes, slides and raindrops), `rock` (steep ground without loose cover, and scoured ground), `water_distance`, and the list of `lakes` (middle, level, area, depth). `TerrainMaps::Sample` and `GetWaterDepth` read them at any place.

- **Repeatable:** one thread, our own random numbers (SplitMix64) and noise, no fast-math. The same settings give the same land to the bit; `terrain_generator_test` generates twice and compares a hash of every map, and also checks a saved file. The debug and release builds gave the same hash.
- **Time and size:** the default 6 x 6 km takes about three minutes in the `release` build (the large scale about two, the raindrops most of the rest). `LoadOrGenerateTerrain(settings, folder, maps, generated, error)` keeps the result in a file named by a hash of the settings and of the generator's version (`kGeneratorVersion`, raised whenever the output changes) and loads it in a fraction of a second; the file is 344 MB (heights and six maps as 32-bit numbers). `forest_scene` and `terrain_tool` keep it in `build/terrain_cache`.
- **The default land:** relief 110 m, valleys branching every few hundred meters, 89% of it gentler than 10 degrees and almost nothing steeper than 25 (the land is soft and old, like the loess uplands around Batorz), two lakes of 0.2 and 0.5 km2, about 8 m deep. No bare rock shows on such land; the rock layer covers only the few steep walls.
- **Why 6 x 6 km at 1 m:** the same as the Batorz map, so terrain drawing, physics and the measured frame times stay comparable; the large-scale stage at 4 m is what keeps the time to minutes (at 1 m it would be 16 times longer).
- **Simplifications:** the river network is fixed by the large-scale grid, so channels narrower than about 8 m come only from raindrops; lakes have no outflow of their own beyond spilling at the rim, and water does not evaporate; there are no glaciers, no rock layers of different hardness and no meandering rivers; streams are not water surfaces yet (only lakes).

## Ground layers

- `TerrainMaterial` mixes up to eight layers (`kMaxTerrainLayers`). Their textures are two texture arrays (`Renderer::CreateTextureArray`, all images of one size: `colors`, `normals`), `tile_sizes` gives each layer's repeat in meters, and two weight images (`weights`, RGBA = layers 0 to 3 and 4 to 7, one pixel per map point, stretched over the whole height map) say how much of each layer lies where.
- `MakeTerrainLayerWeights(maps, rules, count, seed, weights)` fills the weight images from the generator's maps: a `TerrainLayerRule` per layer gives soft ranges (`TerrainRange`: low, high, fade) of slope, height, moisture, sediment, rock, flow (log10 of square meters), distance to water and water depth, optional noise patches (`patch_size`, `patch_cover`) and a `strength`. The conditions multiply, the weights at each point are scaled to add up to 1, and where no rule holds layer 0 covers.
- The shader (`terrain.frag.hlsl`) reads every layer with a weight at the pixel, near and seven times larger as before, and blends them by **height**: each layer stands as high as its weight plus the brightness of its texture there, and only layers within a short step of the highest show. Borders then look like stones poking out of sand rather than a fade. Texture reads use gradients worked out before the branches, so mipmaps stay right where layers change from pixel to pixel.
- Without textures the ground is white, without weights layer 0 covers; the steep color still works (`steep_start_degrees` 90 turns it off when a rock layer covers steep ground).
- Weights are read at the finest level only; very far away they can shimmer a little (TAA hides most of it). In `forest_scene` the layer textures are cooked assets, 2048 x 2048 and block-compressed (colors BC1, normal maps BC5).
- Test: the layer part of `tests/world/terrain_render_test.cpp` and the weights part of `tests/world/terrain_generator_test.cpp`.

## Height maps

- A `HeightMap` is a grid of heights with the same distance (`spacing`, meters) between neighboring points in both directions. x runs along a row, z from row to row; row 0 is the north edge of real data, so north is -Z, as elsewhere in the engine.
- `GetHeight(x, z)` blends the four points around a place; `GetNormal`, `GetSlopeDegrees` (0 level, 45 as steep as it is far), `GetHeightRange`.
- `MakeNoiseHeightMap(width, depth, spacing, seed, hill_size, hill_height)` makes rolling hills that are the same for the same arguments.
- Files: `SaveHeightMap` / `LoadHeightMap` use Poligon's own format, a line of text (`poligon-heightmap 1 WIDTH DEPTH SPACING`) followed by 32-bit floats. A 6000 x 6000 map is 137 MB and loads in a fraction of a second.

## Real elevation data

Source: Poland's Geoportal (GUGiK), the elevation model from airborne laser scanning, one height per meter, bare ground without trees and buildings. The Geoportal says it is free of charge and may be used for any purpose.

- Service (WCS 2.0.1): `https://mapy.geoportal.gov.pl/wss/service/PZGIK/NMT/GRID1/WCS/DigitalTerrainModelFormatTIFF`, coverage `DTM_PL-KRON86-NH_TIFF`.
- Coordinates are in the Polish grid EPSG:2180. In a request, `SUBSET=x(...)` is the **easting** and `SUBSET=y(...)` the **northing**; the other way round gives a file full of zeros and no error.
- `SCALEFACTOR=0.5` returns every second meter.
- The answer is a TIFF with one uncompressed 32-bit float per pixel. `LoadHeightMapFromTiff` reads exactly that and nothing else; it is not a general TIFF reader.
- Ask for pieces of at most 3 x 3 km. One request for 12 x 12 km came back with its eastern half empty.
- A few points come back as 0 ("no data"). `FillMissingHeights` gives them the average of their neighbors.

## The tool

```
terrain_tool join OUT.heights SPACING COLUMNS ROWS FOLDER PREFIX   join tiles PREFIX_c<column>_r<row>.tif, fill pinholes
terrain_tool rescale IN.heights OUT.heights HORIZONTAL VERTICAL    real land -> game land
terrain_tool preview IN.heights OUT.png                            a picture of the relief, lit from the north-west
terrain_tool info IN.heights                                       size, height range, how steep the land is
terrain_tool generate CACHE PREVIEWS [NAME=VALUE ...]              generate (or load) land, write pictures of it and its maps
```

`generate` takes any setting of `TerrainGeneratorSettings` as NAME=VALUE (for example `seed=7 size=2048 erosion_steps=100`) and writes `relief.png` (lit from the north-west, lakes blue), `detail.png` (the middle 1024 x 1024 m at one pixel per meter), `flow.png`, `moisture.png`, `sediment.png` and `rock.png`. It is how the generator is tuned: a 2 x 2 km land takes 20 seconds.

`rescale` with HORIZONTAL 0.5 halves all distances and keeps the heights: a 12 km square becomes 6 km and every slope gets steeper (45 degrees becomes 63). The lowest point is moved to height 0.

## The first real map: Batorz

In `poligon-assets/source/terrain/batorz` (outside the repository):

- `tiles/`: 16 tiles of 3 x 3 km, one height every 2 m, 137 MB, downloaded on 2026-10-14. The square is 12 x 12 km around 50.861443 N, 22.496135 E (EPSG:2180: east 739948 to 751948, north 332549 to 344549).
- `batorz_real_2m.heights`: the tiles joined, 6000 x 6000 points; heights 218.8 to 320.7 m; 21 pinholes filled.
- `tiles_1m/` and `batorz_6km_1m.heights`: the middle 6 x 6 km with a height every meter (4 tiles, 137 MB, downloaded on 2026-10-14; 6000 x 6000 points, heights 226.0 to 316.1 m, no pinholes). **This is the map the game uses, at scale 1:1.**
- `batorz_6km_2m.heights`: the same area cut from the 2 m data; a spare.
- `batorz_preview.png`: the relief: a river valley through the middle and loess gullies on both sides.

How steep it is, from 40000 places:

| | under 10 degrees | 10 to 25 | 25 to 45 | over 45 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| real | 83.6% | 13.9% | 2.4% | 0.1% |
| squeezed to 0.7 | 72.3% | 22.6% | 4.4% | 0.7% |
| squeezed to 0.5 | 59.4% | 30.6% | 7.8% | 2.1% |

The walking character climbs up to 50 degrees, so at 0.5 about a fiftieth of the land is walls: the sides of the gullies.
